opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it wasn't a single moment of revelation. It was more a gradual accumulation of evidence that made the picture hard to avoid.

Back around 2017 and 2018, when some of us at OpenAI were working on AI safety via debate, we were already assuming that the systems we'd eventually need to align would be very capable reasoners that communicate in natural language. Debate only makes sense if you have agents that can argue, make claims, and point to evidence in a way a human judge can follow. At the time that was a somewhat speculative bet. Language models were interesting but not obviously the main line.

Then the scaling results came in. You'd train a bigger model on more text and it would just get better at a surprisingly wide range of things, often things nobody had explicitly trained it for. That told me pretraining was soaking up an enormous amount of latent structure about the world and about human reasoning. But a pretrained model on its own is an imitator. It predicts what a human would write, so at some level it's bounded by the distribution of human text.

The piece that completes the picture is reinforcement learning on top. Once you have a model with that broad base of knowledge and reasoning ability, RL lets you push it toward outcomes rather than imitation. If you can check whether the answer is right, whether the code runs, whether the proof goes through, you can optimise against that signal and the model is no longer limited to what people have already written down. That's the classic recipe from game-playing systems, where self-play took you past human level, combined with a foundation that actually understands a lot about the world.

So the combination looked, to me, like the most plausible path: pretraining gives you breadth and a starting point, RL gives you a way to go beyond the data. And the recent progress on reasoning models has, if anything, made me more confident in that view, not less.

That's also exactly why I worry about it from a safety perspective. The moment you optimise hard against a reward signal, you get whatever the signal actually rewards, not what you meant. In domains where we can verify answers cheaply that's manageable. In the domains we care most about, where humans can't easily check the work, you need something like debate or other scalable oversight methods to keep the training signal honest. So the same reasoning that convinced me this is the path to very capable systems is what convinced me the alignment problem here is real and urgent.

r002.rationale: It discusses models learning human reasoning from pretraining, but does not characterize human reasoning as a collection of heuristics, including heuristics for reasoning itself.

r003.rationale: The response says pretraining supplies breadth and reinforcement learning can push models beyond imitation, but does not state that selectively strengthening good reasoning patterns learned from internet text could suffice for superintelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came gradually, and partly through watching my own assumptions fail. When I was at OpenAI around 2017 and 2018, the thing that struck me about language was that it's this incredibly general interface. If you can do language well, you can in principle talk about mathematics, about code, about plans, about your own reasoning. So language models always seemed like a plausible substrate for something very capable, even when they were still producing mostly nonsense.

What I didn't expect was how far pure prediction would get you on its own. The scaling results, where you just make the model bigger and train it on more text and it keeps getting better at a very wide range of things, shifted my view a lot. It suggested that the pretraining objective was quietly teaching the model a kind of compressed model of the world and of how people reason.

But pretraining alone has a ceiling of sorts. The model is imitating the distribution of text it's seen, so it tends toward the average of what humans write, including the mistakes. That's where reinforcement learning comes in. Once you have a model that already understands the structure of a problem, you can start rewarding it for actually getting the answer right, or for proving the theorem, or for passing the tests, rather than just for sounding like someone who might. And that lets the model move beyond imitation. It can discover strategies that aren't in the training data because the feedback signal is about outcomes, not about matching a human.

The combination is what made me take the superintelligence framing seriously. You have a general-purpose reasoning engine from pretraining, and you have a mechanism for pushing it past human performance in any domain where you can check the result. Mathematics and code are the obvious early cases, because verification is cheap there. But I expect that frontier to broaden, and the models themselves will be used to help build better verification for the harder, fuzzier domains.

I should say this isn't purely a story about optimism. Part of why I moved toward safety work is that reinforcement learning is exactly the ingredient that makes the trajectory worrying. When you optimise hard against a reward signal, you get whatever the signal actually rewards, which may not be what you intended. So I see RL on language models as the thing that both makes superintelligence feel reachable and makes the alignment problem concrete rather than hypothetical. Those two realisations arrived together for me, and I don't think you can hold one without the other.

r003.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning can push pretrained models beyond imitation, but does not specifically present the view that selectively strengthening good reasoning patterns learned from internet text could suffice for superintelligence.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key connection is between learning from what humans have already done and learning by trying things and getting feedback. A language model trained to predict text acquires a lot of knowledge and a surprisingly broad set of skills. But that training objective doesn’t directly ask it to discover better solutions than the ones people have written down.

Reinforcement learning gives you a way to take that starting point and optimise for success at a task. In mathematics or programming, for example, you can sometimes check whether an answer is correct even when finding it is very difficult. So the learning signal doesn’t have to come from a human demonstrating a solution. The model can generate attempts, get feedback, and learn to do better.

That creates a plausible route beyond human performance: you start with the capabilities learned from human text, then improve them through practice on problems where you can evaluate the results. The big question is how far that generalises beyond tasks with clean checks. And that’s also where the alignment problem becomes central, because being able to train a system to achieve an outcome is different from knowing that the outcome you’re rewarding is actually what you want.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key idea was that language gives us a way to combine learning from human knowledge with learning through trial and error. A language model starts with a huge amount of structure acquired from text. Reinforcement learning can then push it to do more of the things that actually work, rather than just imitate what people have written.

The interesting question is where that process stops. I don’t think human performance is an obvious ceiling. In areas where you can check an answer, like mathematics or programming, a system can potentially discover solutions that people wouldn’t have supplied as training examples. You don’t have to know how to produce a solution yourself to recognise that it succeeds.

That makes it a plausible route to capabilities beyond our own. But it also brings the alignment problem into focus: if the system becomes better than us at solving problems, how do we make sure our feedback rewards genuinely good work, rather than work that merely looks good to us? Those two questions—how to get beyond imitation, and how to supervise something more capable than its supervisor—are closely connected.
